subject: Agriculture
title: Legumes Fix Nitrogen
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Legumes Fix Nitrogen.

hook.text: Legumes are the only major crops that manufacture their own fertilizer. They pull nitrogen from thin air.

buildup.text: Rhizobium bacteria colonize legume roots, forming nodules where they convert atmospheric nitrogen to ammonia.

discovery.text: This symbiosis can fix 200 kg of nitrogen per hectare per year—equivalent to a costly fertilizer application.

twist.text: When legumes die, the nitrogen stays in the soil—feeding the next crop. That's why crop rotation works.

climax.text: Before synthetic fertilizer, legumes were the only way to restore soil nitrogen. They're still the cheapest.

punchline.text: Legumes don't just grow food. They grow fertility.

quiz.question: How do legumes contribute nitrogen to the soil?
options: Root bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia the plant can use

details.summary: Legumes partner with rhizobia bacteria to convert atmospheric nitrogen into plant-available ammonia, a process called biological nitrogen fixation. This topic covers the symbiosis, its agricultural benefits, and why legumes reduce the need for synthetic fertilizer.
details.whyItMatters: Nitrogen fertilizer is expensive and polluting. Legumes provide free nitrogen to the soil, improving fertility for subsequent crops and reducing agriculture's environmental impact.
takeaways: Legume root nodules house billions of rhizobia bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen
A legume crop can fix 50–300 kg of nitrogen per hectare per year
Rotating legumes with cereals reduces fertilizer needs for the following crop

faq.question: How do legumes fix nitrogen from the air?
faq.answer: Legume roots form specialized nodules that house rhizobia bacteria. The bacteria convert atmospheric N₂ gas into ammonia using the enzyme nitrogenase, and the plant provides sugars in return—a mutually beneficial symbiosis.

faq.question: Why should farmers include legumes in their crop rotation?
faq.answer: Legumes leave residual nitrogen in the soil after harvest, reducing the need for synthetic fertilizer on the next crop by 25–50%. They also break pest and disease cycles, improve soil structure, and diversify farm income.
